title: Regulators and statutes: who writes the rules, who enforces them, and who insures you

reading.body:
Securities regulation runs as a chain. Each level answers to the one above it.

**Congress** passes the laws, called the Acts. The laws create the **SEC** and give it power. The SEC is a federal agency. It writes detailed rules and oversees the markets.

The SEC oversees **self-regulatory organizations (SROs)**. These are FINRA, the exchanges (NYSE, Nasdaq), and the MSRB. They write industry conduct rules and mostly enforce them. The SROs regulate their **member firms**, the broker-dealers. The firms supervise their **registered reps**.

Read it as a chain: Congress → SEC → SROs → firms → reps. A rep answers to the firm. The firm answers to FINRA. FINRA answers to the SEC. The SEC answers to Congress.

States run a second track, the Uniform Securities Act, called blue-sky law. A rep meets it on the Series 63 or 66. Know the name only.

Two laws carry most of the exam. Keep them straight.

The **Securities Act of 1933** is the "Paper Act" or "Truth in Securities Act." It governs **new issues, the primary market**. That means registration statements, the prospectus, and anti-fraud in offerings. Its job is full and fair **disclosure**. Buyers of new securities can then judge for themselves.

The **Securities Exchange Act of 1934** is the "People Act." It governs the **secondary market**, which is trading after issuance. It **created the SEC**. It requires exchanges and broker-dealers to register, and it makes issuers report (10-K, 10-Q, 8-K). It sets the insider-reporting and anti-fraud rules (10b-5). It gave the **Federal Reserve** its margin power (Regulation T).

Shortcut: **1933 is the paperwork of being born. 1934 is the ongoing life of trading and people.**

reading.h: Who WRITES vs. who ENFORCES — three traps the exam loves
reading.body:
**The SEC never "approves" a security.** It reviews a registration statement for completeness and lets it take effect. It does not pass on the merits, guarantee accuracy, or endorse the investment. Every prospectus must say so. To claim the SEC approved a security is a criminal offense.

**The MSRB writes municipal-securities rules but has NO power to enforce them.** It cannot examine or discipline anyone. **FINRA** enforces its rules for broker-dealers, and **bank regulators** enforce them for bank dealers. The MSRB also cannot regulate the municipal **issuers** themselves. The Tower Amendment forbids it.

**FINRA is an SRO, not the government.** It can censure, fine, suspend, or bar a member or a person. But it **cannot jail** anyone. Criminal cases go to the SEC, the DOJ, and the courts.

reading.h: SIPC vs. FDIC — two different safety nets
reading.body:
**SIPC protects brokerage customers.** The Securities Investor Protection Act of 1970 created it. It steps in when a broker-dealer fails and is shut down. Coverage is **$500,000 per separate customer, of which at most $250,000 may be cash.** It replaces missing cash and securities. It does **not** cover market losses, commodities, futures, or fixed annuities.

A "separate customer" means a separate legal capacity. An individual account and a joint account at the same firm are two customers. Two individual accounts are one customer.

**FDIC protects bank deposits** — checking, savings, and CDs — up to **$250,000 per depositor, per bank, per ownership category.** It never covers securities. A mutual fund, stock, or annuity bought at a bank branch is not FDIC-insured. That is why the "not FDIC insured, may lose value" notice is required.

Keep them straight: **SIPC covers a brokerage failure. FDIC covers a bank failure.**

reading.h: The Federal Reserve: monetary policy and margin
reading.body:
The **Federal Reserve** is the nation's central bank. It is independent of Congress and the President. On this exam it shows up two ways.

First, the Fed runs **monetary policy**. Its tools are open-market operations (buying and selling Treasuries), the discount rate, reserve requirements, and interest on reserve balances. These shape the money supply and interest rates. Buying securities eases policy, so rates fall. Selling securities tightens policy, so rates rise.

Second, the 1934 Act gave the Fed power over **credit and margin**. It writes **Regulation T**, the margin rule at broker-dealers, now a 50% initial requirement. It also writes Regulation U, for bank loans on securities. Note who does what: the **Fed sets** Reg T, and **FINRA and the firms enforce** it and set the tighter maintenance levels.

**Fiscal policy** — taxing and spending — belongs to Congress and the President, not the Fed.

reading.h: The rest of the statute timeline
reading.body:
Beyond 1933 and 1934, learn a short timeline.

The **1939 Trust Indenture Act** covers public corporate debt over $50 million in 12 months. Such debt needs a written indenture and an independent trustee who acts for the bondholders. The **1940 Investment Company Act** covers mutual funds, closed-end funds, and UITs. The **1940 Investment Advisers Act** defines an adviser by the ABC test: Advice, Business, Compensation.

The **1970 SIPA** created SIPC. The **1975 Securities Acts Amendments** created the MSRB and the National Market System and ended fixed commissions. The **2002 Sarbanes-Oxley Act** created the PCAOB for audit oversight and required CEO and CFO certification after the accounting scandals.

Two anti-money-laundering filings round it out, from the Bank Secrecy Act and PATRIOT Act. A firm files a **SAR** (Suspicious Activity Report) for suspicious activity, generally $5,000 or more. A firm files a **CTR** (Currency Transaction Report) for cash of more than $10,000 in one day.

quiz.stem: A FINRA member broker-dealer violates an MSRB rule while selling municipal bonds to a customer. Which body enforces that rule against the firm?
quiz.explanation: The MSRB writes municipal rules but has no enforcement arm; FINRA enforces MSRB rules against broker-dealers (bank regulators do so for bank dealers). Choosing the MSRB is the trap — it writes but never enforces, and under the Tower Amendment it cannot regulate the issuer at all.

quiz.stem: Which of the following statements about SEC review of a securities registration is TRUE?
options: The SEC approves the security once it finds the offering suitable for the public
The SEC guarantees the accuracy of the information in the prospectus
The SEC clears the registration for effectiveness but does not approve the security or pass on its merits
The SEC sets the public offering price it believes is fair
quiz.explanation: The 1933 Act is built on disclosure, not merit review: the SEC lets a registration become effective but never approves a security, guarantees accuracy, or sets price. The 'approves/suitable' and 'guarantees accuracy' choices are exactly the misrepresentations the law makes a criminal offense.

quiz.stem: A customer holds $600,000 of securities and $200,000 of cash in an individual account, and $300,000 of securities in a joint account with her spouse, all at the same broker-dealer. The firm fails and is liquidated. What is the MAXIMUM SIPC coverage?
quiz.explanation: SIPC covers $500,000 per separate capacity (max $250,000 cash). The individual account's $800,000 claim (cash of $200,000 is within the cash sublimit) is capped at $500,000; the joint account is a separate capacity, so its $300,000 is fully covered — $800,000 total. Adding the accounts to $1,100,000 ignores the per-capacity cap.

quiz.stem: Which of the following is protected by FDIC insurance?
options: Shares of a stock mutual fund purchased at a bank branch
Common stock held in a brokerage account
A variable annuity sold by a bank's registered representative
A 12-month certificate of deposit issued by an FDIC-member bank
quiz.explanation: FDIC insures bank deposits — checking, savings, and CDs — up to $250,000 per depositor, per bank, per category. It never covers securities, even bought at a bank; the mutual fund, stock, and annuity are all investment products carrying the 'not FDIC insured, may lose value' disclosure.

quiz.stem: Which statute created the Securities and Exchange Commission and gave the Federal Reserve authority over margin?
options: The Securities Investor Protection Act of 1970
quiz.explanation: The 1934 Act created the SEC, governs the secondary market, and delegated margin/credit authority (Reg T) to the Fed. The 1933 Act is the primary-market disclosure statute and created no agency; it predates the SEC, which is why enforcement of the 1933 Act passed to the SEC once the 1934 Act created it.

quiz.stem: Which body is responsible for setting the initial margin requirement (Regulation T) that applies to broker-dealers?
quiz.explanation: The Federal Reserve writes Reg T (currently 50% initial) under the 1934 Act. FINRA and the firms enforce it and set the tighter maintenance minimums, but they do not set the initial requirement — that division of labor (Fed sets, FINRA/firms enforce) is the tested point.

quiz.stem: A registered representative tells a client that because the firm is a FINRA member and SIPC member, the client's account is protected against a decline in the market value of the securities. This statement is:
options: Correct, because SIPC guarantees against investment losses
Correct, because FINRA membership insures the account
Incorrect, because SIPC covers missing cash and securities if the firm fails but not market losses
Incorrect, because only FDIC insurance can protect a securities account
quiz.explanation: SIPC protects customers if the broker-dealer fails and cannot return their property — it never insures against a drop in market value. The 'FDIC' choice is also wrong because FDIC covers bank deposits, not securities accounts.

quiz.stem: Under the Bank Secrecy Act, a firm that receives a single cash deposit of $15,000 from a customer in one day must file a:
quiz.explanation: A CTR is required for cash transactions exceeding $10,000 in a day, regardless of whether anything looks suspicious. A SAR is triggered by suspicious activity (generally $5,000+), which is not what a routine $15,000 cash deposit alone indicates.
